advisor.summary: Most clients do not have a meals problem; they have a chart-of-accounts problem. Post-TCJA, entertainment is nondeductible under §274(a), business meals survive at 50 percent under §274(n), and a short list of categories — company recreational events for rank-and-file employees, food sold to customers, items available to the general public — stays at 100 percent through the §274(e) exceptions. One blended 'Meals & Entertainment' account produces the wrong answer in both directions: fully deductible items get haircut to 50 percent, and nondeductible entertainment leaks into the deduction. The fix is separated accounts, a receipt habit that captures who and why, and a year-end reclassification pass. The model applies the advisor-computed incremental deduction — enter the after-percentage recovery, never gross spend.
mechanics: §274(a)(1) disallows entertainment outright — tickets, golf, club dues, suites — and Reg. §1.274-11 allows the food at an entertainment event only when purchased separately or separately stated on the invoice.

Business meals hold at 50 percent under §274(n): not lavish, taxpayer or an employee present, provided to a business associate — with Notice 2018-76 and the final regulations confirming client meals survived the TCJA.

The 100 percent lane runs through the §274(e) exceptions: recreational and social events primarily for non-highly-compensated employees, food and beverages sold to customers for adequate consideration, items available to the general public, and meals treated as W-2 compensation.

Substantiation follows §274(d) discipline — amount, date, place, business purpose, and the business relationship of attendees; a card statement alone concedes the deduction, while an annotated receipt defends it.

For amounts paid after 2025, §274(o) makes employer eating-facility and convenience-of-the-employer meal costs nondeductible — on-site meal programs need their own account because their answer changed.

The modeled amount is the incremental deduction recovered by reclassification and documentation at the correct percentages — the advisor computes it from the actual meal accounts, and the engine deducts it exactly as entered.

requirements: Separate ledger accounts for 100 percent, 50 percent, and nondeductible spend (plus eating-facility costs where they exist).
Receipts annotated with attendees and purpose, captured at the time — a ten-second habit, not a year-end project.
A bookkeeper briefed on the categories and sample-checked during the year.
risks: The leading exam pattern is concession by silence: undocumented meals are simply given up, because a §274(d)-style substantiation failure leaves nothing to argue — the annotated receipt is the entire defense.
Entertainment miscoded as meals draws adjustment plus accuracy penalties, and the separately-stated rule for event food is applied literally.
The 100 percent employee-event category requires the event to be primarily for non-highly-compensated employees — an owners' dinner does not qualify.
This strategy recovers deductions on spending that already occurs; presenting it as new savings overstates it — the honest frame is stopping an annual forfeiture.
On-site meal programs lose their deduction in 2026; budgets built on the old treatment will miss.
stateNotes: Conformity: federal-conformity states absorb the meal percentages inside federal business income with no separate computation; a handful decouple on specific §274 items, so confirm each filing state.
PTET interaction: the recovered deduction reduces entity income ahead of any pass-through entity tax computation — the engine sequences PTET after it.
Missouri: conforms through rolling conformity and its federal starting points (RSMo §143.091, §143.121), so the federal meal percentages carry into the Missouri base unchanged.
reviewChecklist: Chart of accounts restructured — the trial balance no longer shows a single blended meals line.

Receipt-annotation habit confirmed operating by sample test, not just instructed.
Eating-facility and convenience-meal costs isolated and excluded from the deduction.

client.teaser: Stop giving away meal deductions your books already earned.
client.headline: Get full credit for the meals your business already buys
plainEnglish: The tax rules for meals are fussy. A client lunch is 50 percent deductible. The office holiday party is 100 percent. Sports tickets are zero. Most businesses throw all of it into one pile in their books.

When everything sits in one pile, the safe move at tax time is to cut it all in half. That means the fully deductible items lose half their value — every single year. And meals with no note about who and why can be lost entirely if the IRS asks.

The fix is simple and permanent. We split your books into the right categories and give you a ten-second receipt habit: snap a photo, note who you were with and why. At year end we check the coding and claim each category at its full allowed rate.
client.analogy: It is like sorting your recycling. Toss everything in one bin and the whole load gets treated as trash. Sort it, and each item keeps its full value.
benefits: Full credit for 100 percent items like the company party
